paras: The lynching of Curtis Shortney was the seizure of a Black prisoner from a freight train near Utica, Mississippi, on September 12, 1888, by a party that was reported to have lynched him. Shortney was accused of taking part in the killing of Dr. L. W. Holliday at Utica about three weeks earlier, a killing for which Bob Broome had already been hanged by lynchers. The wire dispatch said only that it was "supposed" he was lynched, and no report of his body appears in the coverage.

According to a Jackson dispatch printed in the Iuka Reporter, six Black men fired on a group of unarmed white men at Utica in August after a dispute over the sidewalk, and Dr. Holliday was shot through the head. Bob Broom, called the ringleader, was taken from the calaboose by more than a hundred men and hanged near the town cemetery. The same report named "Vice Rainy and Curtis Shortney, brothers," as among the men who fired, said they were still at large and "hotly pursued" by Holliday's friends, and warned there might be more lynching.

Shortney was captured at Rolling Fork, "two miles out," and placed aboard an east-bound freight train. Having learned by telegraph that he was aboard, a lynching party boarded the train at Carpenter. The men ordered Conductor Gordon to stop, and at a point six miles west of Utica they took Shortney off the train. The Raymond dispatch, dated the same day, closed with the words "it is supposed, lynched."

Three weeks later the Pascagoula Democrat-Star, calling him "Justis Shortney, another one of the murderers of Dr. Holliday," reported that a crowd had taken him from the guards on the train and hanged him from a limb. No report of an inquest, of the body being found, or of any arrest of the lynchers appears in the coverage.

The story reached the press as a single Raymond special to the New Orleans Picayune and the Commercial Herald, which ran nearly word for word from New York to Kansas. The New York Sun headed it "Taken from a Train by Lynchers" and the Wichita Eagle "A Supposed Lynching," while the Memphis Appeal and the Greenville Times declared "Curtis Shortney Lynched" and "Shorney Lynched" over text that still said only "supposed." The Atlanta Constitution placed it in a "Crimes and Criminals" column under "The Same Fate Befell Him," linking it to Broome's hanging.

Every version stated as fact that Shortney had been "engaged with Bob Broome" in the killing, and none named the lynchers. Mississippi weeklies reduced it to one line in their state-news columns, the Brookhaven Leader repeating the "supposed" and the Pascagoula Democrat-Star reporting a hanging. Copying introduced variants, including "Shartneys" and "Brooke" in Savannah and "six miles east of Utica" and "Bennett" in Emporia.

reader.title: Lynching of Curtis Shortney
bases: A lynching party stopped a freight train, took off a Black prisoner accused in the killing of a white physician, and was reported to have lynched him (A10, A11, A18).

A 'lynching party' took Shortney from a train over the killing of Dr. Holliday (A10, A11); the September dispatches say only that it was 'supposed' he was lynched (A10, A14, A16), and only a later state-news brief says he was hanged (A18).

The seizure rests on one Raymond dispatch (the Picayune/Commercial Herald special) reprinted widely (A10, A11, A14); the only statement that he was hanged is an unsourced later brief (A18), and no report of a body or inquest appears.

accounts.label: Raymond wire dispatch (Picayune / Commercial Herald special)
accounts.gist: A lynching party that learned by telegraph Shortney was aboard boarded the freight at Carpenter, had the conductor stop the train six miles west of Utica, and took him off; 'it is supposed' he was lynched.

accounts.label: Mississippi state-news brief
accounts.gist: Shortney, 'another one of the murderers of Dr. Holliday', was arrested at Rolling Fork; a crowd boarded the train, took him from the guards and hanged him from a limb.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Raymond dispatch nearly verbatim, stating the accusation ('engaged with Bob Broome in the killing') as fact and the lynching as 'supposed'.
The Memphis Appeal and Greenville Times headlined the death as accomplished ('Curtis Shortney Lynched', 'Shorney Lynched') though their text said only 'supposed'.
The Pascagoula Democrat-Star called him 'another one of the murderers of Dr. Holliday' and reported the hanging as fact in a one-line state-news item.

conflicts.note: The contemporaneous Raymond dispatch does not confirm a death; the later Pascagoula brief gives no source and misnames him 'Justis'.
Same dispatch, different wording; the date Sept. 12 is not in dispute.
